drills.title: The locked front gate
drills.briefing: Someone rotated the webhook secret on the Git host this morning. Since then, every push is turned away before the pipeline can start.

failure.message: Push event rejected: signature verification failed (HTTP 401).
details: Webhook secret last rotated on the Git host: 2 hours ago

drills.hint: Read the two signature lines. Why would the same payload produce a different signature?

choices.label: Update the webhook secret in the CI settings so it matches the one on the Git host
choices.why: The signature is an HMAC of the payload made with a shared secret. After a rotation both sides must hold the same value, or every delivery is rejected.

choices.label: Turn off signature verification so deliveries are accepted
choices.why: That removes authentication: anyone could trigger your pipeline with a forged push. Never trade security for a green build.

choices.label: Increase the webhook timeout on the Git host
choices.why: The request was not slow; it was rejected with a 401. Timeouts do not affect signature checks.

choices.label: Re-push the same commit until it goes through
choices.why: Every retry is signed with the new secret and fails the same way.

drills.explanation: The receiver computes an HMAC-SHA256 of the request body with its stored secret and compares it to the header. When only one side was rotated, the two signatures can never match.
drills.lesson: Rotate secrets on both ends together, and treat a 401 at the trigger as a credentials problem rather than a code problem.

drills.title: Works on my machine
drills.briefing: A teammate's checkout feature builds perfectly on their laptop. The pipeline disagrees.

failure.message: Build failed: Module not found: Can't resolve './CheckoutSummary' in '/runner/work/src/pages/checkout'.
details: npm ERR! code ELIFECYCLE · exit status 1

drills.hint: Compare the import with the file name the build suggests. What differs?

choices.label: Make the import match the file's exact name: './checkoutSummary'
choices.why: Linux file systems are case-sensitive; macOS and Windows usually are not. The import has to match the real file name exactly.

choices.label: Clear the dependency cache and rebuild
choices.why: The missing module is your own source file, not a package. A clean cache cannot change a file name.

choices.label: Upgrade the runner's Node.js version
choices.why: Module resolution behaves the same across supported Node versions; the file simply is not found under that spelling.

choices.label: Add the checkout folder to the bundler's resolve paths
choices.why: The folder already resolves, since the error names it. The casing of the file name is what fails.

drills.explanation: The developer's laptop treats CheckoutSummary and checkoutSummary as the same file. The Linux runner does not, so the import points at a file that does not exist.
drills.lesson: CI is the first honest test of your file names. Match casing exactly, and consider enabling a lint rule for case-sensitive imports.

drills.title: The gate that said no
drills.briefing: Tests are green and the build is fine, but the security gate refuses to let this release continue.

failure.message: Security gate failed: 1 high-severity vulnerability found.
details: lodash@4.17.15 · prototype pollution · severity HIGH · fixed in 4.17.21

drills.hint: The scan already tells you which version fixes it.

choices.label: Upgrade lodash to the patched 4.17.21 and refresh the lockfile
choices.why: The vulnerable code is replaced by a fixed release, so the finding disappears for the right reason.

choices.label: Add the advisory to the ignore list
choices.why: An ignore list hides a known hole instead of closing it. It is only acceptable with a documented risk acceptance and an expiry date, not as a quick unblock.

choices.label: Lower the policy threshold to 'critical' only
choices.why: Changing the gate so the failure no longer counts is not a fix. The vulnerable code still ships.

choices.label: Skip the security stage for this release
choices.why: Bypassing the gate sends the vulnerability onward. Gates exist to stop exactly this.

drills.explanation: A transitive dependency pulled in an old lodash. Upgrading to the fixed version removes the vulnerable code rather than silencing the scanner.
drills.lesson: Fix the finding, not the gate. If a patched version exists, upgrading is almost always the cheapest correct answer.

drills.title: Fails only after midnight
drills.briefing: A date-grouping test passes locally, fails on the runner, and only for orders placed just after midnight.

details: Runner timezone: UTC · Author's laptop: Asia/Kolkata (UTC+05:30)

drills.hint: Look at the last line. What differs between the two machines?

choices.label: Make the code and the test use explicit UTC dates instead of the machine's local timezone
choices.why: Once the date logic no longer depends on where it runs, it gives the same answer on every machine.

choices.label: Re-run the job until the test passes
choices.why: This is not random flakiness. It fails deterministically whenever the runner's timezone differs from the author's, so retrying only burns minutes.

choices.label: Increase the test timeout
choices.why: Nothing timed out. An assertion compared two different dates.

choices.label: Delete the test because it only fails in CI
choices.why: A test that fails in CI is revealing a real environment dependency. Deleting it removes the safety net and leaves the bug.

drills.explanation: The code groups orders using the local timezone. Five and a half hours of offset moves orders near midnight into the previous day on a UTC runner.
drills.lesson: Never let tests depend on the clock or timezone of the machine. Inject time, or pin everything to UTC.

drills.title: One repo too many
drills.briefing: The main repository clones fine. A private submodule added yesterday stops the checkout cold.

failure.message: fatal: could not read Username for 'https://git.example/acme/design-tokens.git': terminal prompts disabled.
details: fatal: clone of 'https://git.example/acme/design-tokens.git' into submodule path failed
Main repository checkout: OK · Submodule checkout: FAILED

drills.hint: Which credential does the runner have, and which repositories does it cover?

choices.label: Give the runner read access to the private submodule repo with a deploy key or a repo-scoped token
choices.why: The runner's credential only covers the main repository. A read-only, least-privilege credential lets it clone the submodule without a person at the prompt.

choices.label: Commit the submodule's files directly into the main repository
choices.why: It works, but it throws away history and ownership, and the real problem (the runner lacking access) returns with the next private dependency.

choices.label: Turn off submodule checkout and build without it
choices.why: The build needs those design tokens. This trades a checkout error for a confusing build error later.

choices.label: Use a personal admin token with full account access
choices.why: It would work, but a broad personal token on a shared runner is a serious leak risk. Prefer read-only, repo-scoped credentials.

drills.explanation: Cloning a private repository needs credentials. CI has no human to type them, so the runner must be given a narrowly scoped one.
drills.lesson: Every new private dependency needs an access plan for CI. Give pipelines the least privilege that gets the job done.

drills.title: Healthy in Dev, dead in Staging
drills.briefing: The image is identical to the one that passed Development. Staging refuses to become healthy.

failure.message: Deployment failed: readiness probe returned 503 for all replicas.
details: storefront-web: Error: DATABASE_URL is not defined
Container exited with code 1 · restarted 3 times

drills.hint: Same image, different outcome. What else differs between the two environments?

choices.label: Add the DATABASE_URL secret to the Staging environment's configuration and redeploy
choices.why: Configuration is per environment. The app crashes on start because Staging never received the variable that Development has.

choices.label: Scale Staging up to more replicas
choices.why: Every replica crashes for the same reason. More replicas only means more crash loops.

choices.label: Extend the health check timeout
choices.why: The container exits with code 1 before it could ever answer. Waiting longer changes nothing.

choices.label: Rebuild the image from scratch
choices.why: The same code worked in Development, so the image is not broken. The environment is missing configuration.

drills.explanation: The application reads DATABASE_URL at start-up. In Staging it is undefined, so the process exits and the readiness probe never succeeds.
drills.lesson: Build once, configure per environment. A failing start-up with a missing variable is almost always an environment config gap, not a code bug.

drills.title: Killed within seconds
drills.briefing: This release adds an in-memory search index. The new pods start, then vanish within seconds, and the rollout stalls.

failure.message: Deployment failed: container OOMKilled (exit code 137) during start-up.
details: storefront-web-7c9d: State: Terminated · Reason: OOMKilled · Exit Code: 137
Release notes: product search index is now loaded into memory at boot

drills.hint: Exit code 137 with OOMKilled has one meaning. Compare the limit with the peak.

choices.label: Raise the container memory limit to fit the new index, then watch real usage after the deploy
choices.why: Exit code 137 with OOMKilled means the kernel killed the process for exceeding its memory limit. The new release legitimately needs more than 256Mi.

choices.label: Restart the pods
choices.why: They will load the same index and hit the same limit. A restart resets the clock, not the cause.

choices.label: Lengthen the readiness probe delay
choices.why: The pod is not slow to become ready; it is killed before it can be. Probe timing does not change the memory limit.

choices.label: Remove the memory limit entirely
choices.why: That deletes the guard rail: one leak could then starve the whole node. Right-size the limit instead of removing it.

drills.explanation: The peak (255Mi) sits right at the 256Mi limit. Loading the index at boot pushes memory over the line and the kernel kills the container before it can serve traffic.
drills.lesson: When a release changes what is held in memory, its resource limits must change with it. Check limits whenever you see exit code 137.
